name: Diphencyprone (DPCP)

lead: Diphencyprone (DPCP) is a topical chemical that dermatologists apply to the scalp to provoke a mild, controlled allergic reaction. In alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy hair loss, this is used to try to redirect the immune attack on hair follicles and restore hair.

It is also used for warts. Reviews of alopecia areata treatments include contact immunotherapy, and trials going back to the 1980s have reported regrowth in some patients, with results varying widely between studies.

paras: It is applied in a clinic or under specialist supervision: first to sensitise a small area, then in a regular weekly routine to a part or all of the scalp, with the strength adjusted to keep a mild reaction. Regrowth, when it occurs, is generally reported over months.

Expected effects include itching, redness and eczema-like inflammation at the site, and more severe reactions or blistering can occur. It is not a self-treatment: it is handled by dermatologists and is not a standard retail product.

chain: Mild allergic reaction changes local immune activity
Hair follicles may resume growth in alopecia areata
angle.text: DPCP is used to regrow hair lost to alopecia areata, including extensive patterns. It is a clinic-supervised treatment for autoimmune hair loss, not for pattern baldness.

lead: Diphencyprone (DPCP) is a topical contact allergen used as 'contact immunotherapy' for alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy hair loss, and for stubborn viral warts. [1][2] Applied to the scalp under medical supervision, it causes a deliberate mild dermatitis that is thought to change the local immune response around the follicle.

For appearance, its role is regrowth: patients with patchy or extensive scalp hair loss use it to try to recover hair. Cochrane reviews list contact immunotherapy among the treatment categories assessed in alopecia areata trials. [1][3] Controlled trials from the 1980s and later studies in different populations have examined it. [4][5][6]

In wart treatment, a 2021 meta-analysis pooling 14 studies and 851 patients reported a random-effects pooled cure rate of 75.5%, with high heterogeneity. [7] It has also been studied topically for in-transit melanoma metastases, a medical rather than cosmetic use. [8]

paras: Alopecia areata affects about 0.15% of people at a time and can range from small patches to total scalp or body hair loss; treatments include immunosuppressants, hair-growth stimulants and contact immunotherapy. [1][3] DPCP is one of the contact immunotherapy agents.

Contact allergens including DPCP are widely used for stubborn warts; a review describes dinitrochlorobenzene, DPCP and squaric acid dibutylester as the most frequent agents. [2] A 2012 Cochrane review covers topical treatments for warts more broadly. [9]

Early controlled studies reported DPCP in alopecia areata, including a 1983 trial and a 1986 placebo-controlled comparison of therapies in patchy disease. [5][6] A 1998 study examined Indian patients. [10] A randomised trial compared DPCP with anthralin in extensive chronic alopecia areata. [11] Cochrane reviews of alopecia areata interventions assess the overall trial evidence. [1][3]

In warts, a meta-analysis found a pooled cure rate of 75.5% with high heterogeneity between studies. [7] A randomised pilot trial added DPCP to standard treatment in cutaneous leishmaniasis, and a meta-analysis examined it for melanoma in-transit metastases. [4][8]

As a contact sensitiser it intentionally causes dermatitis at the site; the wart-treatment review describes adverse effect profiles as differing slightly between agents and says all can be used safely when guidelines are followed. [2]
